```text
=== #39 ===

Export a budget month | open | jamesleonard3rd | ['scope: large'] | 2026-09-13T21:05:01Z | comments: 0
## Summary
There is no way to get a budget month out of the application. The budget page header has no export or print action, so a user who wants to share a month's budget with a partner, bring it to a financial advisor, or keep a record outside the app has to screenshot it. Individual reports have export paths, but the budget screen itself has none.

## User Story
As a user that that would like a way to have a concise and comprehensive paper copy of my budget to show to others, I want to be able export the current budget month as a file (CSV for data, PDF/print for a readable snapshot) so that I can share or archive it without screenshotting the screen. The export should reflect what's on the budget page — categories, budgeted, spent, and remaining — for the selected month.

## Acceptance Criteria

1.  The budget page header(top right) has an **Export** action with CSV and PDF options for the selected month
2.  The export lists every visible category group and category with Budgeted, Spent, and Remaining, matching the budget page exactly, with group subtotals and totals
3. The CSV opens cleanly in spreadsheet apps, and the PDF/Print version is a clean, readable single-month snapshot without app navigation

## Out of Scope


## Open Questions

## Rough Scope
Medium-Large:

Derived from common user need to bring or send a report to a financial advisor.

=== #4 ===

Net Worth Summary Card | open | bennettmatuszewski | ['scope: medium'] | 2026-09-04T14:23:06Z | comments: 2
## Summary

Actual Budget tracks balances across checking, savings, loans, and credit cards, but there is no single view that shows net worth (assets minus liabilities) at a glance. A Net Worth summary card on the accounts overview page — pulling from already-loaded account balances and broken down by asset accounts vs. liability accounts — would give users an immediate read on their overall financial position without navigating account by account.

## User Story

As a user on the accounts overview page, I want to see my total assets, total liabilities, and net worth in a summary card so that I can understand my overall financial position at a glance without adding up account balances myself.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A summary card appears at the top of the accounts overview page showing three values: Total Assets, Total Liabilities, and Net Worth.
2. Total Assets is the sum of all positive-balance account types (e.g., checking, savings, investments); Total Liabilities is the sum of all liability account types (e.g., credit cards, loans); Net Worth is Total Assets minus Total Liabilities.
3. All three values update immediately when any account balance changes on the page, with no additional user action required.
4. Each value is formatted consistently with the currency and decimal conventions used elsewhere in Actual.
5. Net Worth is visually distinguished when negative (e.g., displayed in red) to make an at-a-glance deficit obvious.
6. The card is visible without scrolling on typical desktop viewports and reflows gracefully on narrow viewports without truncating values.
7. If an account is hidden or excluded from totals by the user, it is also excluded from the summary card calculations.

## Out of Scope

- A full Net Worth over time report or chart.
- Filtering the summary by date range or custom account groupings.
- Including off-budget accounts in the totals.
- Any new backend endpoints — all values must be derived from balances already loaded in the accounts overview.
- Exporting or sharing the summary card.

## Open Questions

1. Should off-budget accounts (e.g., a tracking account for a mortgage) be included, excluded, or optionally toggleable? This affects both the arithmetic and the UI.
2. Is there an existing summary or header component on the accounts page this card should slot into, or does it need to be a net-new component placed above the account list?
3. Should the card be collapsible or dismissible for users who do not want it? If so, should that preference persist across sessions?
4. How should accounts with a zero balance be treated in the asset vs. liability breakdown — counted in assets, ignored entirely, or shown separately?

## Rough Scope

Medium — The arithmetic is simple and account balances are already in memory, but for a beginner team finding where to slot a new component into the accounts page, understanding the data flow to that component, and matching Actual's existing visual style and component conventions all add meaningful time on top of the core logic.

## Source

Derived from a common feature request; scoped down from a full Net Worth report to stay frontend-only. Assisted with Claude for issue generation.
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-09-29 19:09:07Z)**_

Written for: your teammates and the instructor/TA reviewing the issue on GitHub.

```markdown
## Summary
There is no way to get a budget month out of Actual. The budget page header has no export or print action, so a user who wants to share a month's budget with a partner, bring it to a financial advisor, or keep a record outside the app has to take a screenshot. Export already exists elsewhere (CSV from the Budget Analysis report and from account transactions), but the budget screen itself has none.

## User Story
As a user who wants a concise, complete copy of my budget to show to others, I want to export the selected budget month as a CSV (for data) or a PDF (for a readable snapshot) so that I can share or archive it without screenshotting the screen.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The budget page header (top right) has an **Export** action that opens a menu with **CSV** and **PDF** options.
2. Both exports cover only the month currently selected on the budget page. If multiple months are displayed, the user can choose which month to export.
3. The export lists every visible category group and category in the same order as the budget page, with **Budgeted**, **Spent**, and **Balance** columns.
4. Each category group has a subtotal row, and the export ends with a grand total row.
5. All values match the budget page for that month, including carryover balances.
6. Amounts use the same currency and number formatting the user has configured in Actual.
7. The CSV has a header row, uses standard comma separation and quoting, and opens correctly in Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice (category names containing commas or quotes do not break columns).
8. The PDF is a single-month snapshot with the budget file name and month as its title, and contains no app navigation, sidebars, or buttons.
9. The PDF stays readable when it runs past one page: table rows are not cut in half, and column headers repeat on each page.
10. Downloaded files are named `<budget-name>-<YYYY-MM>.csv` / `.pdf`.
11. Export works in both the browser and desktop (Electron) versions.

## Out of Scope
- Exporting more than one month or a date range in a single file.
- Exporting reports, transactions, or account data (those have their own paths).
- Excel (.xlsx) or other formats beyond CSV and PDF.
- The mobile budget page.
- Scheduled, emailed, or otherwise automatic exports.
- Customizing which columns are included or how the PDF looks.
- Any new sync-server endpoints; everything is generated on the client.

## Open Questions
1. **Budget modes:** Envelope and tracking budgets use different components and summary values. Should both be supported in the first version, or only envelope?
2. **Hidden categories:** Should hidden categories and groups be left out (matching the default page view), or follow the page's current "show hidden" toggle?
3. **Income:** Should income categories be included, and in envelope mode, should the "To Budget" / overbudgeted summary appear at the top?
4. **PDF approach:** Should we generate a real PDF file (which needs a new client-side library, a dependency decision for the team), or use a print stylesheet plus the browser/Electron "Save as PDF" dialog? The second is simpler but gives less control over the output.
5. **Code reuse:** Can the CSV builder in `components/reports/spreadsheets/budget-analysis-export.ts` be generalized, or should the budget export have its own builder?

## Rough Scope
Large. The CSV half is moderate: the budget values are already in the budget spreadsheet, and Budget Analysis has an existing CSV export pattern to follow. The PDF half is what makes this large. The codebase currently has no printing or PDF generation, so we have to choose an approach and possibly add a dependency (Open Question 4), build a print-specific layout, handle page breaks, and make sure it works in both browser and Electron. Supporting both budget modes (Open Question 1) and matching carryover/subtotal logic exactly adds testing effort on top of that.

## Source
Derived from a common user need to bring or send a budget report to a financial advisor or partner.
```

```markdown
## Summary
Sub-issue of #39. This covers only the **CSV** half of budget month export. PDF export is left to a separate sub-issue.

The budget page has no way to get a month's data out of Actual. This issue adds an Export action to the budget page header that downloads the selected month as a CSV, so users can open it in a spreadsheet app, share it, or archive it. Actual already exports CSV from the Budget Analysis report and from account transactions, so this follows an existing pattern.

## User Story
As a user who wants to share or keep a record of my budget, I want to export the selected budget month as a CSV file so that I can open it in a spreadsheet app or send it to someone without screenshotting the screen.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The budget page header (top right) has an **Export** action. For now it offers only **CSV**, and it should be built so a PDF option can be added later without redesigning it.
2. The CSV covers only the month currently selected on the budget page. If multiple months are displayed, the user can choose which month to export.
3. The CSV has a header row and lists every visible category group and category in the same order as the budget page, with **Budgeted**, **Spent**, and **Balance** columns.
4. Each category group has a subtotal row, and the file ends with a grand total row.
5. All values match the budget page for that month, including carryover balances.
6. Amounts are plain numbers without currency symbols or thousands separators, and use the user's configured decimal places, so spreadsheet apps can treat them as numbers.
7. The file uses standard comma separation and quoting, and opens correctly in Excel, Google Sheets, and LibreOffice (category names containing commas or quotes do not break columns).
8. The file is named `<budget-name>-<YYYY-MM>.csv`.
9. Export works in both the browser and desktop (Electron) versions.
10. The CSV builder has unit tests covering subtotals, totals, carryover, and escaping of special characters.

## Out of Scope
- PDF or print export (separate sub-issue of #39).
- Exporting more than one month or a date range in a single file.
- Excel (.xlsx) or other formats.
- Exporting reports, transactions, or account data.
- The mobile budget page.
- Customizing which columns are included.
- Any new sync-server endpoints; everything is generated on the client.

## Open Questions
1. **Budget modes:** Envelope and tracking budgets use different components and summary values. Should both be supported here, or only envelope?
2. **Hidden categories:** Should hidden categories and groups be left out (matching the default page view), or follow the page's current "show hidden" toggle?
3. **Income:** Should income categories be included, and in envelope mode, should "To Budget" / overbudgeted appear as a summary row?
4. **Code reuse:** Can the CSV builder in `components/reports/spreadsheets/budget-analysis-export.ts` and its save-file call in `BudgetAnalysis.tsx` be generalized, or should the budget export have its own builder?

## Rough Scope
Medium. There is an existing CSV export pattern to follow (Budget Analysis builds a CSV string and passes it to the platform save-file call), and the budget values are already in the budget spreadsheet on the client, so no backend work is needed. Most of the effort is in collecting the right values for one month across groups and categories, getting subtotals and carryover to match the page exactly, adding the header action, and writing tests. Supporting both budget modes (Open Question 1) would push this toward the high end of medium.

## Source
Split from #39 to deliver CSV export separately from the more complex PDF export.
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-09-29 19:15:06Z)**_

It depends on how the PDF gets made. That's Open Question 4 from the #39 draft, and it's the main thing driving the size.

**Print stylesheet plus the browser's "Save as PDF": medium.**
- The CSV sub-issue already builds the month-selection logic, the subtotal/total calculation, and the Export action in the header. The PDF work can reuse all of that.
- What's left is a print-only layout: hide the navigation and sidebars, keep table rows from splitting across pages, and repeat the column headers on each page.
- No new dependency is needed. Browsers and Electron both have a print dialog with "Save as PDF."
- The downside is less control. The user has to go through the print dialog, the output looks a little different in each browser, and the filename can't be forced.

**A generated PDF file from a library: large.**
- The team has to agree to add a dependency, which is a big decision in a codebase that currently has no PDF or printing code.
- The layout has to be built again inside the library, separately from the budget table's existing components. Page breaks, fonts, currency formatting, and long category names all have to be handled by hand.
- A true one-click download works differently in the browser than in Electron, so it has to be built and tested on both.

**My recommendation:** write the PDF sub-issue as **medium, using the print-stylesheet approach**. In Out of Scope, list "a directly generated PDF file (no print dialog)." If the team wants that later, it can be its own large follow-up. This also means the PDF sub-issue should list the CSV sub-issue as a dependency, since it reuses the data and header work.

Taken together, the two medium sub-issues still add up to the large parent issue.

_**User (2026-09-29 19:17:36Z)**_

explain the two different approaches more simply

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-09-29 19:17:43Z)**_

**Approach 1: Print the page (medium)**

You tell the browser how the budget should look when printed. For example: hide the menus and buttons and show only the table. The user clicks Export → PDF, the normal print window opens, and they choose "Save as PDF."

- Easier, because the browser does the hard part of making the PDF.
- The user has to go through the print window, and the result can look a little different in each browser.

**Approach 2: Build the PDF yourselves (large)**

You add a PDF tool (library) to the project and write code that draws the file: the title, the table, each row, and where each page breaks. The user clicks Export → PDF and the file downloads directly.

- Smoother for the user: one click, and it looks the same everywhere.
- Much more work. The team has to agree on adding the library, rebuild the table layout from scratch inside it, and handle details like long names and page breaks that the browser would otherwise take care of.

**In short:** Approach 1 lets the browser make the PDF, and Approach 2 has you make it yourselves. That's why the first one is medium and the second is large.

**Title:** Export a budget month as PDF
**Label:** `scope: large`
**Parent:** #39

```markdown
## Summary
Sub-issue of #39. This covers the **PDF** half of budget month export, and depends on the CSV sub-issue (#<CSV issue number>).

Users who want to bring a budget month to a financial advisor or share it with a partner need a clean, readable document, not a spreadsheet. This issue adds a **PDF** option to the budget page's Export action that directly downloads a formatted PDF of the selected month, with no print dialog. The PDF is built by a PDF library added to the project, so it looks the same in every browser and in the desktop app.

## User Story
As a user who wants a readable copy of my budget to show to others, I want to export the selected budget month as a PDF file so that I can print, share, or archive it without screenshotting the screen.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The budget page's Export action (added in the CSV sub-issue) has a **PDF** option next to CSV.
2. Choosing PDF directly downloads a `.pdf` file, with no print dialog, named `<budget-name>-<YYYY-MM>.pdf`.
3. The PDF covers only the selected month and uses the same data as the CSV export: every visible category group and category in page order, with **Budgeted**, **Spent**, and **Balance** columns, group subtotals, and a grand total.
4. All values match the budget page for that month, including carryover balances.
5. Amounts are formatted with the user's configured currency and number format, the same way they appear in the app.
6. The PDF has a title showing the budget file name and month, and contains no app navigation, sidebars, or buttons.
7. Group headers and subtotal/total rows are visually distinct from category rows (for example, bold text or shading).
8. When the budget runs past one page, table rows are not split across pages, column headers repeat at the top of each page, and pages are numbered.
9. Long category names wrap or shorten cleanly without overlapping other columns.
10. The PDF looks the same when exported from Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and the desktop (Electron) app.
11. The PDF library is loaded only when the user exports a PDF, so it does not slow down the app's normal startup.
12. There are unit tests for turning budget data into the PDF table rows (order, subtotals, totals, formatting).

## Out of Scope
- Anything already covered by the CSV sub-issue (month selection, data collection, the Export action itself).
- A print-stylesheet / "Save as PDF" through the print dialog approach.
- Exporting more than one month or a date range in a single PDF.
- Charts, graphs, or notes in the PDF.
- Customizing the PDF's layout, colors, columns, or branding.
- The mobile budget page.
- Any new sync-server endpoints; the PDF is generated on the client.

## Open Questions
1. **Which library?** Options include jsPDF (with the jspdf-autotable plugin for tables), pdfmake, or @react-pdf/renderer. The team needs to compare them on bundle size, table and page-break support, license, and how well they fit a React/TypeScript codebase, then get the choice approved before implementation starts.
2. **Fonts and characters:** Built-in PDF fonts may not display every currency symbol or non-English category name. Do we need to embed a font, and how much would that add to the download?
3. **Budget modes:** Should the PDF support both envelope and tracking budgets, matching whatever the CSV sub-issue decides?
4. **Summary section:** In envelope mode, should "To Budget" / overbudgeted appear at the top of the PDF?
5. **Saving on desktop:** Should the Electron app use the same download behavior as the browser, or the platform save-file dialog that CSV export uses?

## Rough Scope
Large. Actual currently has no printing or PDF code, so this adds a new dependency, and that decision needs research and team approval (Open Question 1). The budget table's existing React components can't be reused inside the PDF, so the layout has to be rebuilt in the library, including styling, column widths, wrapping long names, page breaks, repeated headers, and page numbers. Fonts and currency symbols may need extra work (Open Question 2), and loading the library only on demand plus checking the output across browsers and Electron adds testing time. The data work is already done by the CSV sub-issue, so this is large because of rendering, not data.

## Source
Split from #39. Chosen over the simpler print-dialog approach so users get a consistent, one-click PDF download.
```

Notes:
- Fill in `#<CSV issue number>` once you've created the CSV sub-issue. You can also mark it as "blocked by" that issue on GitHub.
- Open Question 1 is the one to settle first. Adding a dependency to Actual is a team decision, and the library you pick affects most of the other criteria.
- AC11 (load the library only when needed) is there because PDF libraries can be large. It's also easy for a reviewer to check.
